1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.
6	
7	A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.
8	
9	The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.
10	
11	To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.
12	
13	The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

content.content:
1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
22	
23	The jaw carriages
24	
25	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.
26	
27	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
28	
29	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
30	
31	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
32	
33	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
34	
35	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
36	
37	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
38	
39	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
40	
41	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
42	
43	An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.
44	
45	Operation
46	
47	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
48	
49	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
50	
51	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

Here is my invention.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

lines: FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

-The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

+The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left and one at the right. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each crosses the inner boundary of that body and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. Those circumferential positions and their apportionment between the frame halves are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically; the inner face of that member is a concave arc meeting the outer surface of the pipe 90, its depth shown schematically. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the annular frame body at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. content.content:
1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

The disclosure separates two events: 'When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring' and, separately, 'closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face'. The install sequence confirms the order: close the frame, then move the latch to holding, then over-center. The candidate sentence made the faces meet only when the latch was also engaged, which contradicted its own lead-in ('the same motion that closes the frame halves'), its own Operation paragraph, claim 1's 'engaging one another as the first frame half and the second frame half are closed', and claim 13's separation of closing-and-coupling from 'moving the latch to a first position'. Deleting four words restored one consistent account of the crux relationship, which is the relationship the whole application turns on, so a written-description mismatch there would have been the worst place to leave one.

I declined to touch the other sentence containing 'the latch 16 is engaged' (line 5 of the Detailed Description). It says the two halves define an annular frame when brought together and latched. That is a statement about the frame being held closed by the releasable latch, which the disclosure supports directly, and it makes no claim about the cam ring. Rewriting accurate text to make a keyword check quieter would have been a loss, so I left it and said why.

The minor finding was also genuine and was a real render risk, not a paperwork nit: two sheets show the same clamp, FIG. 4 expressly specifies the over-center attitude, and FIG. 1's brief specified nothing about the lever, so the pipeline could have produced FIG. 1 latched-open next to FIG. 4 latched-over-center while the text asserted over-center for both. The over-center position itself is source-supported ('a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe'), so naming the state adds no new technical content; I kept the lever's exact attitude a depiction convention marked 'shown schematically' so no page geometry leaks back into the patent text.

Fixing the figure forced a second, unrequested repair I had to make anyway: the addition pushed FIG-1.md past the 2800-character ceiling. I bought the space back inside that one brief rather than by dropping the new sentence or by deleting a numeral. Every trim was wording only, not content: I merged the joint-line and frame-half sentences, tightened the carriage apportionment clause, moved 'the jaw pad 40' forward so the second reference could become 'its', and compressed the section-line sentence. The eight listed numerals, all targets, the clamped-jaw geometry, the schematic markings and the 3-3 cutting plane are untouched, so the sheet renders the same drawing.

No claim was amended this turn. The fixes moved the description toward the claims rather than the claims toward the description, which is the right direction when the two disagree and the claims already track the disclosure: claim 1 and claim 13 were the correct texts here, and the prose was the outlier.

The prior-art set is empty, so nothing in this turn was shaped by a reference and there was no citation trace to redo. Claim 1's distinguishing feature therefore rests on the disclosure alone, and it is the feature the fix protects: a cam ring split with the body whose segments are re-coupled at both the hinge end and the latch end by the closing motion itself, so a single latch input reaches all three carriages through one kinematic element. -FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

+FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer removed over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. Two bodies occupy the upper and lower parts of the view. Each is bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by an arc concentric with it, and each ends toward the middle of the view at a straight end face that runs from the left boundary to the right boundary. The two end faces face one another across a narrow gap. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body lies a hatched block that follows the two arcuate boundaries, is spaced inward from each of them, and reaches down to the end face of that body. That block is the first cam ring segment 22.

Both findings are fixed and every file is back in sync.

**Terminology finding (minor).** `draft/08-detailed-description.md` ¶5 now reads "define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame", matching the single directional term defined in ¶1 and used by the Brief Description and every figure brief. There is now one name for that axis throughout.

**FIG. 4 finding (major).** FIG. 4 no longer shows the cam ring ending in free space or the latch bridging one frame half. The brief now specifies a second hatched frame body at the lower right holding a further arcuate band of like width, a narrow radial gap between the two frame bodies, the two band ends meeting in that gap along complementary surfaces facing one another circumferentially and in contact, both bands together being the segmented cam ring 20, and the latch housing 58 reaching across both bodies.

The reviewer's literal fix would have put eleven numerals on FIG. 4 (its existing eight plus 10, 22 and 28), over the eight-per-sheet ceiling. So I identified the mating structure on a focused sheet instead of overcrowding FIG. 4: the abutting segment end and the far frame half appear on FIG. 4 as unnumbered context bodies described without their canonical part names, and new **FIG. 6** is an enlarged detail of the latch-end joint carrying five numerals: first frame half 10, second frame half 12, first cam ring segment 22, second cam ring segment 24, and the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28. Its handedness was checked against the other sheets: viewed from FIG. 1's side with radially outward to the right, the upper body is the first frame half holding segment 22 and the lower is the second frame half holding segment 24, which matches FIG. 1's upper/lower halves and FIG. 2's upper/lower segments meeting at faces 28 on the right.

Synchronized with that: `draft/07-drawings.md` gains a FIG. 6 entry, and the cam ring section of the Detailed Description gains one sentence stating what FIG. 6 shows, in the same terms the claims and the numeral table use. No numeral was added, removed or redefined, no claim or disclosed embodiment changed, and no part was deleted from any sheet.

Two constraints I had to work inside while editing FIG. 4: the added geometry pushed the brief to 3197 characters, so I condensed the view note, the schematic-convention list and several sentences back to 2775, keeping every body, contact, opening and relationship; and FIG. 4's numeral 16 now targets a physical surface (the outer surface of the enclosure's left wall) rather than "the assembly as a whole, outside the enclosure", which pointed at open space. All six briefs are now at or under 2800 characters with eight or fewer numerals each, no em dashes, and no notes or placeholders anywhere.

reasoning: The FIG. 4 finding was a real state inconsistency, not a labeling nit: the brief fixed the view as the closed, over-center latch end, and in that state the description says faces 28 are closed on one another and both segments rotate as one ring, yet the sheet drew one band stopping under the housing with nothing beyond it. Left alone the render would have contradicted the crux relationship of the invention at exactly the joint that carries it.

I could not apply the reviewer's suggested fix verbatim. Adding 10, 22 and 28 to FIG. 4 would have made eleven numerals on one sheet against a hard ceiling of eight, and the sheet was already at eight. The drafting rules give the answer for that case: add a focused detail sheet rather than overcrowd, and carry the structure the old sheet still needs as unnumbered generic bodies. So FIG. 4 now draws the abutting band and the far frame body as 'a further band of like width' and 'a second hatched body', with no canonical part name and no numeral, and new FIG. 6 identifies the same joint properly with five numerals.

I checked FIG. 6's handedness against the sheets it has to agree with before writing it, because a detail that disagrees with its parent view is worse than no detail. Viewed from FIG. 1's side with radially outward toward the right, the latch joint puts the first frame half above and the second below, which matches FIG. 1's upper and lower halves and FIG. 2's upper segment 22 and lower segment 24 meeting at faces 28 on the right. No rotation or mirroring was needed, so FIG. 6 required no new orientation convention.

FIG. 6 was appended as the sixth figure rather than inserted after FIG. 4, which would have renumbered the mounting-boss sheet to FIG. 6 and forced edits to its file, its Brief Description entry and two places in the Detailed Description. Appending keeps the Brief Description in numerical order and touches two files instead of five, and a detail figure appearing after the views it details is ordinary practice.

I deliberately kept FIG. 6 to the joint alone and stated that no structure outside the frame at the joint is shown. Numbering the annular guide 18 there would have meant drawing guide walls in a view along the axis, where the guide opens toward the viewer, and would have added a sixth numeral for no gain; 18 is already carried by FIG. 3 and FIG. 5.

Adding geometry to FIG. 4 broke the 2800-character ceiling, so the trimming was forced work, not tidying. Every cut was wording: shortened view and orientation notes, a compressed schematic-convention list, and merged sentences. The bodies, the gap, the contact at the joint, the frame-wall interruption, the wedge bearing on the drive face, the spring symbol, the handle attitude and the indicator pin all survive, and the eight numerals are unchanged.

One endpoint changed while I was rewriting FIG. 4: numeral 16 pointed at 'the assembly as a whole, outside the enclosure', which is open space and cannot be verified by a leader check. It now points at the outer surface of the enclosure's left wall, a physical target distinct from 58's top-wall hatching. Nothing else about the latch's depiction changed.

Nothing was taken from the pixels or from the reviewer's description of them into the invention. The two unnumbered context bodies added to FIG. 4 are structure the disclosure already states, one cam ring segment carried by each frame half meeting at complementary faces at the latch end, so no embodiment, numeral definition or claim was widened to accommodate a drawing.
